Action Plan:
1) Prescribe replacement inhalers for asthma control: salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler as needed for wheeze/shortness of breath and beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler as maintenance therapy (dose/route/frequency not documented). Prescriptions to be available within approximately 1 hour.
2) Start a short course of oral steroids to treat current asthma exacerbation: take tablets for 5 days, 2 tablets in the morning; side effects discussed (mood changes, high blood sugar, rash, nausea, headaches). Read medication label.
3) Provide a spacer device and written instructions; encourage use with inhalers to optimize delivery.
4) Safety-net advice: if needing salbutamol more often than every 3 hours at any time, or if symptoms worsen (increasing shortness of breath, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness), seek urgent medical attention.
5) Rest advised; time off work appropriate. Patient can self-certify for up to 7 days.
6) Follow usual care after improvement: resume maintenance inhaler consistently; use salbutamol as needed for wheeze.
Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Acute chest tightness.
- History of present illness:
  - Chest tightness for approximately 3 hours.
  - Mild shortness of breath (not at rest), worse with exertion (stairs).
  - Wheeze and slight, non-productive cough; cough slightly worse at night and persistent.
  - Recent upper respiratory infection last week (sore throat, runny nose), nasal symptoms improving; cough persists.
  - No chest pain; describes tightness and difficulty taking a full breath.
- Past medical history:
  - Asthma since childhood; severe exacerbation requiring intubation at ~16–17 years.
  - Allergic rhinitis/hay fever; dust allergy.
  - Childhood eczema; childhood milk protein allergy.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler PRN — ran out ~1 week ago; not used in past week (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler — ran out ~1 week ago; not used in past week (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Mother with eczema; father with asthma.
- Social history: University student. Tobacco/alcohol/drug use not documented.

Objective:
- Telehealth consultation; no physical examination performed.
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Respiratory status by history: not short of breath at rest; exertional dyspnea; wheeze and chest tightness reported; non-productive cough.
- Investigations: None performed; no peak flow available.

Assessment & Plan:
1. Acute chest tightness/wheeze with exertional dyspnea:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (High) — supported by DDx: “Acute asthma exacerbation (likely viral-triggered and worsened by lapse in controller/reliever use)” [High likelihood].
   - Differential diagnosis:
     - Post-viral bronchial hyperreactivity/acute viral bronchitis [Medium] — recent URI with persistent cough supports.
     - Community-acquired pneumonia [Low] — lacks fever, sputum, pleuritic pain.
     - Pulmonary embolism [Low] — acute dyspnea possible but no risk factors or classic features; wheeze and known asthma more consistent.
     - Spontaneous pneumothorax [Low] — no sudden pleuritic unilateral pain or severe rest dyspnea.
   - Investigations planned: None during this consult.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented).
     - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler as maintenance (dose/route/frequency not documented).
     - Oral steroids: 5 days, 2 tablets each morning; side effects discussed.
     - Provide spacer and usage instructions.
     - Safety-net: seek care if salbutamol is needed more often than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen (worsening SOB, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness).
     - Rest and time off work; self-certify up to 7 days.
   - Relevant referrals: None at this time; advised to seek urgent care/ED if red flags occur.

2. Medication refill and adherence:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Loss of asthma control due to lapse in controller (ICS) and reliever (SABA) use for ~1 week — supported by DDx item “Loss of asthma control due to lack of controller medication” [Impairment factor].
   - Differential diagnosis: Not applicable.
   - Investigations planned: None.
   - Treatment planned: Reissue prescriptions; reinforce adherence and consistent maintenance inhaler use; spacer technique education.
   - Relevant referrals: None.

3. Work/school absence:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Requires rest during recovery from acute asthma exacerbation.
   - Investigations planned: None.
   - Treatment planned: Rest; patient may self-certify for up to 7 days.
   - Relevant referrals: None.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals, pulse oximetry, or peak flow recorded; no physical exam; exact inhaler doses/route/frequency not documented; steroid medication name and tablet strength not documented; smoking status and exposure history not documented; no scheduled follow-up arranged; inhaler technique not directly assessed.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief audio cutouts occurred during discussion of steroid side effects.
